description.narrative: Tajikistan Millati Solim Project for Tajikistan has the development objectives to improve the quality and efficiency of Primary Health Care (PHC) services in selected districts and to strengthen the national capacity to respond to public health emergencies. Component 1: Quality Improvements of Primary Care through PHC Strengthening supports national policy work and investments in 16 high-poverty districts to make PHC facilities service-ready. Sub-components include Sub-component 1.1, which strengthens human resources and stimulates demand by reviewing and implementing retention and optimization policies for family medicine doctors and nurses in rural areas, delivering six-month in-person family medicine training and PHC management training, establishing a national online platform for Continuous Medical Education (CME), updating curricula to include Gender Based Violence (GBV), antimicrobial resistance, and climate modules, conducting citizen engagement and health promotion including SMS outreach, and fielding an annual national patient survey on PHC experience; and Sub-component 1.2, which improves physical and digital infrastructure through rehabilitation and where needed construction of priority district and rural facilities, provision of basic medical and laboratory equipment and information technology, development of energy-efficient standard designs and alternative power solutions such as solar panels, and piloting mobile PHC service delivery for remote areas. Component 2: Efficiency-Enhancing Reforms in the PHC Network lays the foundations for strategic purchasing and digitalization, conceived for national rollout and implemented first in pioneer regions (Dushanbe and Sughd). Sub-components include Sub-component 2.1, which establishes a Health Services Purchasing Structure as a single purchaser, develops and costs a single state-guaranteed PHC benefit package, revises staffing norms and provider autonomy regulations, develops accreditation for PHC providers, prepares a service delivery network masterplan, designs a contracting and blended provider payment model, and supports a domestic resource mobilization and change management roadmap; and Sub-component 2.2, which implements digital tools through an Electronic Patient Registry (EPR) integrated with the civil registry, a basic Electronic Medical Record (EMR) in PHC facilities, a PHC management dashboard and business intelligence and electronic payment systems, and targeted facility upgrades in pioneer regions to meet accreditation, with performance-based conditions to incentivize results. Component 3: Health Emergency Preparedness and Response (HEPR) strengthens the State Sanitary Epidemiological Service (SES) and national systems by assessing capacities, updating standard operating procedures and sanitary aviation concepts, developing PHC facility emergency plans, training PHC workers, epidemiologists and public health officials, strengthening laboratory networks and border entry points, improving community risk communication and the 511 hotline, costing a National Action Plan for International Health Regulations (IHR 2005), procuring a limited emergency stockpile and rehabilitating warehouses, and conducting annual multi-sector simulation exercises. Component 4: Project Management, Coordination, and Results Monitoring supports implementation, fiduciary and safeguards functions, establishes a Health Analysis Unit (HAU), strengthens the Ministry of Finance on health financing, and delivers biannual Rapid Cycle Facility Phone Surveys (FASTR) and baseline/endline Service Delivery Indicators (SDI) surveys to track service-readiness and quality. Component 5: Contingent Emergency Response enables rapid reallocation of project resources to support response and early recovery in the event of an eligible crisis.

The objectives of the Project are to (i) improve the quality and efficiency of primary healthcare services in selected districts and pioneer regions, and (ii) strengthen the national capacity to respond to public health emergencies.

title.narrative: Number of doctors having completed 6-month family medicine training in selected districts (cumulative)

comment.narrative: The target value for this indicator in 2025 is 140 doctors trained (cumulative), which requires an additional 83 doctors to complete training in 2025.
